record_type_quote: In this study, we replicated Experiment 2 from Raymond, Shapiro, and Arnell’s (1992) seminal paper that made the attentional blink phenomenon famous (the phenomenon was first revealed by Broadbent & Broadbent, 1987, and Weichselgartner & Sperling, 1987).

targets.authors: Raymond, J. E., Shapiro, K. L., & Arnell, K. M.
targets.title: Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: An attentional blink?
targets.evidence_quote: In this study, we replicated Experiment 2 from Raymond, Shapiro, and Arnell’s (1992) seminal paper that made the attentional blink phenomenon famous (the phenomenon was first revealed by Broadbent & Broadbent, 1987, and Weichselgartner & Sperling, 1987).
targets.outcome_quote: From a statistical point of view, the results of our experiment largely replicated the specific pattern of results of Raymond et al. (1992), but they also showed some differences. Specifically, the differences concerned the absolute level of performance and a difference in the onset, peak, and offset of the blink that were found one lag earlier in comparison to those observed by Raymond et al. (1992).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors distinguish preserved blink magnitude and width from statistically substantive differences in accuracy and timing, repeated in Experiment 2. Expert ratings treat the replication as successful, but are reported as expert judgments contrasted with the authors’ statistical comparisons. No unqualified author verdict overrides the explicit mixture. Experiment 2 also repeats within-paper Experiment 1; that is not an additional published target.

reasoning: Verified full article title and all five authors. Two fresh samples re-test Experiment 2 of the 1992 paper; other earlier attentional-blink papers are historical background, not additional targets.
